title: The jewel of peace
hook: Sukhmani means the jewel of peace; many read it daily or in groups when life is hard
carry: resting in the middle of it

segments.voice: Yesterday, sukhasan, the position of rest; your line was sleep in praise. Today a new bani begins, and it will stay with us a while.

A family has just moved into a new house. Boxes still line the hall, but before the furniture is in place, a few relatives sit together on the floor, each holding a small book, reading aloud in a low, steady rhythm. The same scene can turn up the night before an exam, in the month after a funeral, in a week of bad news; sometimes it's a circle of neighbors who meet every week to do just this. They're reading Sukhmani Sahib, a bani Sikh families turn to when life is hard, and when it's new.
screen: `A NEW HOUSE, BOXES IN THE HALL.` → `PEOPLE READING ALOUD TOGETHER.` → `THE BANI THEY REACH FOR: SUKHMANI.`

segments.voice: Sukh means peace, comfort, ease, the opposite of dukh, pain. Mani means a jewel; some also hear man, the mind, in it. So Sukhmani is the jewel of peace, or the peace of the mind. Sahib is added out of respect. It was composed by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, who wrote Sohila's last hymn and compiled the scripture. Tradition says he wrote it at a quiet pool near Amritsar called Ramsar, around the time the scripture was being gathered. It's in Raag Gauri, beginning on Ang 262 of the Guru Granth Sahib. And it's long: twenty-four sections, each opening with a short salok, followed by eight stanzas. Near the beginning, Guru Arjan names the bani himself. In paraphrase: Sukhmani, the jewel of peace, is the nectar of God's Name; it rests in the minds of the devoted. Notice what that says peace is. Not a feeling you chase, or a place you reach once the problems are solved. Peace is the Name, remembering God, and it rests in a mind the way a jewel rests in a box. That's why families open it when life is hard. The hospital room doesn't change. The test is still tomorrow. But the Sikh hope is that something steady can rest in the middle of it. Over the next hundred days, we'll walk through Sukhmani section by section.
screen: `SUKH: PEACE. MANI: A JEWEL.` · `GURU ARJAN, AT RAMSAR.` · `TWENTY-FOUR SECTIONS, EIGHT STANZAS EACH.` · `PEACE RESTS IN A MIND.` · then, large: `THE JEWEL OF PEACE.`

segments.voice: Picture one of those living rooms, people side by side, books open, voices low, or play the first minute of a Sukhmani Sahib recording, just for the sound. Let the steadiness reach you, and find one tight place in your body and let it soften. If you pray, say Waheguru once.
Sukhmani. The jewel of peace: Guru Arjan's long bani of twenty-four sections, read daily by some Sikhs and in groups when life is hard.
Your line: resting in the middle of it. The hard thing stays; something steady can rest there too. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Sikhs read Sukhmani Sahib daily, often in the morning, and families and sangats gather to read it together in times of illness, grief, celebration and new beginnings, such as moving into a new home.

Weekly Sukhmani Sahib groups of women: widely observed; phrased generally. Confirm.
